query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: A severe thermomechanical processing intervention—specifically, heavy cryo‐rolling followed by an optimized annealing treatment—can refine and decompose the uniform lamellar microstructure of the as‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to generate ultrafine recrystallized grains and coherent nanoprecipitates, thereby simultaneously increasing strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion performance for fastener applications under extreme service conditions. This effect is achieved through enhanced dislocation accumulation and controlled phase decomposition that improve interphase interactions.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast, uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy with coupled fcc (L12) and B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Implement a single processing step consisting of heavy cryo‐rolling with substantial deformation followed by an optimized short-term high-temperature annealing treatment to induce targeted microstructural refinement and controlled phase decomposition.
generation.conditions: Designed for fasteners exposed to wide temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loads with room-temperature creep challenges, and corrosive environments (e.g., marine or chloride-containing conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: A heterogeneously refined lamellar structure featuring ultrafine recrystallized domains and coherent precipitates at phase boundaries that enhance interphase interaction and dislocation blockage.
generation.mechanism: The severe cryo-rolling introduces high dislocation densities while the subsequent annealing triggers controlled phase decomposition. This process refines the lamellae into thinner, more heterogeneous domains where geometrically necessary dislocations accumulate at new phase boundaries, increasing back-stress and strengthening. The formation of coherent precipitates additionally contributes to precipitation strengthening, improves creep resistance by impeding dislocation movement, and provides more stable interfaces that also enhance corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting, as-cast alloy, the treated material is expected to exhibit a 20–40% increase in yield and ultimate tensile strength, a multiplication (roughly 2×) of ductility (fracture elongation), significantly reduced creep rates at room temperature, and improved resistance against corrosive attack.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics of the uniform as-cast fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, which shows mechanical properties below industrial requirements for fasteners.
generation.boundary: The improvements are anticipated under conditions typical for fastener applications: moderate to high temperatures (operational stability up to ~700°C), quasi-static and dynamic loading environments, room-temperature creep testing, and exposure to corrosive media (e.g., artificial seawater).
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative gains in strength, ductility, and corrosion resistance depending on the exact processing parameters and scale-up effects remain to be fully determined. Optimizing the processing window will be critical to balance gains across the multiple performance aspects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy specimens: one batch processed by the proposed cryo-rolling plus annealing route and one control batch in the as-cast state. Characterize their microstructures using TEM and EBSD to verify refinement, recrystallization, and nanoprecipitate formation. Conduct standardized tensile tests, long-term room-temperature creep tests, and corrosion tests in simulated marine (chloride-containing) conditions. The experiment should compare strength, ductility, creep rate, and corrosion performance between the two batches.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (via tensile tests)
Creep strain rate at room temperature
Corrosion rate and passivation behavior (electrochemical tests)
Microstructural analysis (grain size, precipitate distribution via EBSD/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed specimens fail to exhibit statistically significant improvements (for example, less than a 20% increase in yield/ultimate strength and less than a doubling of ductility, along with no measurable gains in creep and corrosion resistance) compared to the as-cast control, then the hypothesis that the proposed processing intervention enhances performance under the defined service conditions is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: These results showed that the yield strength (1437 ± 26 MPa), tensile strength (1562 ± 33 MPa), and elongation (14 ± 1%) of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy after annealing at low temperature were significantly improved compared with the as-cast alloy. Eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit an excellent balance of toughness and strength at room temperature. However, there is still an immediate requirement to design structural components with more strength and ductility due to the increasing technical requirements and harsher operating environments in industrial applications. The demand for stronger and more ductile structural elements has increased as airplane components have become more demanding and technical standards have advanced. Therefore, it is of significance to develop a new eutectic high-entropy alloy with superior properties based on AlCoCrFeNi2.1.

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
